passage: Before the advent of modern refrigeration and global supply chains, preserving food through fermentation was a vital survival strategy across nearly every civilization. By encouraging beneficial bacteria and yeasts to convert sugars into acids or alcohol, communities transformed perishable harvests like cabbage, milk, and soybeans into nutritious staples that could last through harsh winters. Beyond extending shelf life, fermentation unexpectedly enhanced flavor complexity and improved digestibility by breaking down tough plant fibers and antinutrients. Today, nutritional scientists have rediscovered what traditional food cultures knew intuitively: fermented foods enrich the gut microbiome, supporting immune function and metabolic health. What began as a practical necessity for preventing spoilage has thus endured as a cornerstone of both culinary heritage and preventive wellness.
